mcqs.question: Why does total() belong on Invoice rather than some other class?
options: It reads only Invoice's own fields (items, taxRate) and needs nothing from outside
Because Invoice is the first class defined in the file
Because it returns a double, and only Invoice methods return doubles
mcqs.explanation: The data test says a method belongs where the data it operates on lives — total() only touches Invoice's own fields. Access level, file order, and return type have no bearing on ownership.

mcqs.question: Per the compare table, what's the concrete tell-tale sign of feature envy?
options: A chain of getter calls into another object's fields, rather than direct access to its own class's fields
The method has more than three parameters
The class implements more than one interface
mcqs.explanation: Feature envy shows up as a method reaching into another object's data via its getters instead of using its own class's fields. Access level, parameter count, and interface count aren't the diagnostic signal here.

mcqs.question: Why is a growing utility class full of domain-specific static methods (like order/customer pricing logic) usually a design smell?
options: Static methods are always slower than instance methods
It's genuinely fine — utility classes should hold as much domain logic as needed
That domain-specific logic has real data it should be operating on as state, and is exactly the kind of behavior that should become its own real class
Utility classes cannot be unit tested at all
mcqs.explanation: Domain-specific logic usually has real state it should own, which is exactly what a static-only utility class can't provide — it should be extracted into a proper class instead. There's no inherent speed cost to statics, and utility classes are perfectly testable; the issue is cohesion, not either of those.

mcqs.question: Why is "just add it to OrderManager, that's where order logic already lives" a risky default?
options: Because Manager classes are forbidden by the SOLID principles
Because OrderManager can only hold up to a fixed number of methods
Because static analysis tools automatically reject Manager-named classes
Because defaulting to a convenient catch-all class, rather than applying the data test, is exactly how Manager classes become bloated dumping grounds with no real cohesion
mcqs.explanation: Skipping the data test in favor of "it's already there" is precisely the pattern that turns Manager classes into unmaintainable catch-alls. SOLID doesn't literally forbid the name, and there's no method-count limit or tooling rejection involved.
